questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Work function of the metal is
options: Maximum possible energy acquired by an electron
Minimum energy required by an electron to just eject from metal surface
Maximum energy which is given to electron to move out of metal surface
questions.solution:
The work function of a metal is defined as the minimum amount of energy required by an electron to just escape from the metal surface.

It is a characteristic property of the metal and varies from one metal to another.

Answer: Minimum energy required by an electron to just eject from metal surface

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Variation of photoelectric current with anode potential is shown below. Choose the correct option ($V_0$ = stopping potential)
questions.solution:
In the photoelectric effect, the variation of photoelectric current with anode potential has the following characteristics:

1. At zero anode potential, there is still some photoelectric current because the emitted photoelectrons possess initial kinetic energy and can reach the anode.

2. When a negative (retarding) potential is applied to the anode, the photoelectric current decreases. It becomes zero at a specific negative potential known as the stopping potential ($-V_0$).

3. As the positive anode potential is increased, the photoelectric current increases because more electrons are accelerated towards the anode.

4. Eventually, all emitted photoelectrons reach the anode, and the current reaches a maximum constant value called the saturation current. Further increasing the anode potential does not increase the current.

Graph-I correctly depicts all these features: it starts from zero at the stopping potential on the negative x-axis, has a positive value at zero potential, and flattens out to a constant saturation current at higher positive potentials.

In photoelectric effect, the maximum kinetic energy of emitted photoelectrons depends on the frequency of incident
radiation. We have
$K E=h v-\phi$
Where $\phi$ is work function, which is the minimum energy required to remove electrons from the metal plate; $f$ is frequency

Therefore, $(K E)_{\max } \propto f$.

questions.q:
A proton and an \( \alpha \) particle are accelerated through the same potential difference \( V \). The ratio of
their de-Broglie's wavelength is
questions.solution:
The de Broglie wavelength is defined as
\[ \lambda=\frac{h}{\sqrt{2 m q V}} \]
Now, for proton \( \lambda_{p}=\frac{h}{\sqrt{2 m_{p} q V}} \)
For \( \alpha- \) particle, \( \lambda_{\alpha}=\frac{h}{\sqrt{2 m_{a} q_{a} V}} \)
Since
\[ m_{p}=4 m, q_{p}=e ; m_{\alpha}=4 m, q_{\alpha}=2 e \]
Ratio of their de Broglie wavelengths is
\[ \frac{\lambda_{p}}{\lambda_{a}}=\frac{\sqrt{m_{a} q_{a}}}{\sqrt{m_{p} q_{p}}}=\frac{\sqrt{4 m \times 2 e}}{\sqrt{m \times e}}=\sqrt{8}=2 \sqrt{2} \]

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
The half life of a radioactive substance is \( 20 \) minutes. The time taken between \( 50 \% \) decay and
\( 87.5 \% \) decay of the substance will be
questions.solution:
Given, half-life of radioactive substance, \( T_{\frac{1}{2}}=20 \) minutes
Using
\[ \begin{array}{l} N=N_{0} e^{-\lambda t} \Rightarrow \frac{N}{N_{0}}=e^{-\lambda t} \Rightarrow-\lambda t=\ln \left(\frac{N}{N_{0}}\right) \\ \Rightarrow t=-\frac{1}{\lambda} \ln \left(\frac{N}{N_{0}}\right) \end{array} \]
We know \( \frac{1}{\lambda}=\frac{T_{1 / 2}}{\ln 2} \)
\[ t=\frac{-\ln 2}{T_{1 / 2}} \ln \left(\frac{N}{N_{0}}\right) \]
If \( t_{1} \) is time for \( 50 \% \) decay and \( t_{2} \) is time for \( 87.5 \% \) decay, we have
\[ \begin{array}{l} t_{2}-t_{1}=-\frac{T_{1 / 2}}{\ln 2} \ln \left(\frac{N_{2}}{N_{0}}\right)+\frac{T_{1 / 2}}{\ln 2} \ln \left(\frac{N_{1}}{N_{0}}\right) \\ =\frac{T_{1 / 2}}{\ln 2}\left(-\ln N_{2}+\ln N_{0}+\ln N_{1}-\ln N_{0}\right)=\frac{T_{1 / 2}}{\ln 2}\left(\ln N_{1}-\ln N_{2}\right) \\ =\frac{T_{1 / 2}}{\ln 2} \ln \left(\frac{N_{1}}{N_{2}}\right) \end{array} \]
Substituting the values, we get
\( t_{2}-t_{1}=\frac{20 \mathrm{~min}}{0.693} \ln \left(\frac{50}{12.5}\right)=\frac{20}{0.693} \times \ln 4=40 \) minutes
Therefore, time taken between \( 50 \% \) decay and \( 87.5 \% \) decay will be \( 40 \) minutes.

questions.q:
A microscope is having objective of focal length \( 1 \mathrm{~cm} \) and eyepiece of focal length \( 6 \mathrm{~cm} \). If tube
length is \( 30 \mathrm{~cm} \) and image is formed at the least distance of distinct vision, what is the
magnification produced by the microscope ? Take D \( =25 \mathrm{~cm} \).
questions.solution:
Given, focal length of objective, \( f_{o}=1 \mathrm{~cm} \); focal length of eyepiece, \( f_{e}=6 \mathrm{~cm} \); length of tube, \( L=30 \)
Using
\( M=\frac{L}{f_{0}}\left(1+\frac{D}{f_{e}}\right)=\frac{30}{1}\left(1+\frac{25}{6}\right)=30(1+4.166) \) \( \Rightarrow M=155=150 \)
Therefore, magnification produced by the microscope is, approximately, \( 150 \).
